sourceNote: Free PDF published by Melbourne University Sport; no copyright or reproduction notice in the document. Run intervals at RPE 4-5 unless marked. Only the timings are recorded; credit and link to the PDF. Week numbers follow the PDF's day grid (3 run days a week).
whoItsFor: Beginners building from zero to 5 km, especially students and staff after a structured, university-backed plan.
howToRun: Three run days a week with a rest day, easy walk or mobility class between them.
Comfortable pace (RPE 4-5 out of 10) unless the session says otherwise.
Not running yet? Swap the run intervals for fast walking. Already run a bit? Lift intervals to RPE 6-7.
Can't run outdoors? Ride a bike instead: push the work intervals, pedal easy on recoveries.

name: NHLBI Sample Walking Program – Week 1
description: A 15-minute starter walk: 5 minutes easy, 5 minutes brisk, 5 minutes easy.

exercises.name: Brisk walk
exercises.weight: target heart-rate zone / can talk, breathing harder

credit: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) – Your Guide to Physical Activity and Your Heart
sourceNote: US federal government publication (NIH Pub. No. 06-5714), public domain. Sample programs on pp. 27-29. Credit NHLBI. The guide sets intensity by target heart-rate zone; we show it as talk-test effort too.
whoItsFor: Inactive adults and older adults starting from scratch, including people over 40 who haven't exercised for a while.
howToRun: Aim for brisk walking on at least 5 days this week.
Brisk = breathing harder but still able to talk; check your pulse sits in your target zone if you use one.
Each week the brisk section grows by about 2 minutes (Week 12: 30 minutes).
Check with your GP first if you have a heart condition or take blood-pressure medicine.

name: NHLBI Sample Walking Program – Week 12
description: The final week of the 12-week walking program: 30 minutes of brisk walking between easy warm-up and cool-down walks.

exercises.name: Brisk walk
exercises.weight: target heart-rate zone / can talk, breathing harder

credit: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) – Your Guide to Physical Activity and Your Heart
sourceNote: US federal government publication (NIH Pub. No. 06-5714), public domain. Sample programs on pp. 27-29. Credit NHLBI. The guide sets intensity by target heart-rate zone; we show it as talk-test effort too.
whoItsFor: Walkers who have built up through the program and can now walk briskly for 30 minutes.
howToRun: Walk briskly on at least 5 days a week.
As fitness improves, walk in the upper half of your target heart-rate zone.
From week 13, keep building brisk time from 30 towards 60 minutes on most days.
Over 40 and ready to jog? NHLBI suggests starting its jogging program at Week 3 after this.

name: NHLBI Sample Jogging Program – Week 4
description: Walk-jog session from the NIH heart guide: two rounds of a 4-minute walk and 5-minute jog.
credit: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) – Your Guide to Physical Activity and Your Heart
sourceNote: US federal government publication (NIH Pub. No. 06-5714), public domain. Sample programs on pp. 27-29. Credit NHLBI. The guide sets intensity by target heart-rate zone; we show it as talk-test effort too.
whoItsFor: Adults moving from walking to jogging, including over-40s who have completed the NHLBI walking program first.
howToRun: The guide suggests jogging on at least 5 days a week; most beginners do better with 3-4 and rest days between.
Warm up with a 5-minute walk and stretch; cool down with a 3-minute walk and 2 minutes of stretching.
Jog in your target heart-rate zone - if you can't talk, slow down.
Repeat a week before moving on if it felt hard.

name: NHLBI Sample Jogging Program – Week 10
description: One 4-minute walk then a 13-minute continuous jog - the program's first long, unbroken jog.
credit: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) – Your Guide to Physical Activity and Your Heart
sourceNote: US federal government publication (NIH Pub. No. 06-5714), public domain. Sample programs on pp. 27-29. Credit NHLBI. The guide sets intensity by target heart-rate zone; we show it as talk-test effort too.
whoItsFor: Walk-joggers about two-thirds of the way through the 16-week NHLBI program.
howToRun: Jog most days the guide suggests; keep at least one or two rest days if you're new.
Weeks 11-12 grow the jog to 15 then 17 minutes; by week 15 it's 20 minutes of jogging.
Stay in your target zone - slow jogging is still jogging.
Afterwards, build jogging time gradually from 20 to 30 minutes (or up to 60).

name: NHS Beginners Walking Plan – Week 1 Walk
description: Ten minutes at a comfortable pace, wrapped in a slow 10-minute warm-up and cool-down.
credit: Wirral Community Health and Care NHS Foundation Trust
sourceNote: Free NHS trust leaflet (PDF), no reproduction restriction stated. Every scheduled walk is wrapped in a 10-minute slower warm-up and 10-minute cool-down. The intermediate plan is already in sourced-programs.json.
whoItsFor: Anyone starting to walk for health - including older adults, people returning after illness and those with low fitness.
howToRun: Three walks this week with a rest day between each.
Comfortable = you could chat the whole way.
The plan adds a fourth walk in week 2 and introduces medium-pace walks in week 4.
By week 10 you'll be doing 35-40 minute walks and short brisk walks six days a week.

name: NHS Advanced Walking Plan – 75-min Long Walk
description: The advanced plan's longest walk: 75 minutes at a comfortable pace plus warm-up and cool-down.
credit: Wirral Community Health and Care NHS Foundation Trust
sourceNote: Free NHS trust leaflet (PDF), no reproduction restriction stated. Every scheduled walk is wrapped in a 10-minute slower warm-up and 10-minute cool-down. The intermediate plan is already in sourced-programs.json.
whoItsFor: Regular walkers who already walk 45 minutes or more most days and want a long, steady walk each week.
howToRun: Appears from week 8 of the advanced plan, up to three times a week alongside medium and brisk walks.
Comfortable pace - this is about time on your feet, not speed.
Take water on warm days and pick a route with somewhere to stop.
Weekly rhythm: long comfortable walks, 55-60 min medium walks and one 30-40 min brisk walk.

name: NHS Advanced Walking Plan – 40-min Brisk Walk
description: A sustained 40-minute brisk walk, the hardest walk in the advanced plan (week 10).
credit: Wirral Community Health and Care NHS Foundation Trust
sourceNote: Free NHS trust leaflet (PDF), no reproduction restriction stated. Every scheduled walk is wrapped in a 10-minute slower warm-up and 10-minute cool-down. The intermediate plan is already in sourced-programs.json.
whoItsFor: Fit walkers who want a harder cardio session without running.
howToRun: Brisk walks start at 30 minutes in week 3 and reach 40 minutes by week 10.
Do it once or twice a week, not on back-to-back days.
Brisk = breathing hard enough that you can only speak in short phrases.
Pair with the 75-minute comfortable walk for a well-rounded walking week.

name: Interval Walking Training (3 min fast / 3 min slow)
description: The Japanese interval walking method: alternate 3 minutes of fast walking with 3 minutes of slow walking, five or more times.

exercises.name: Fast walk
exercises.weight: ≥70% peak walking capacity (puffing, hard to talk)

credit: Shinshu University – Nose H, Masuki S et al. (Interval Walking Training)
sourceNote: Research protocol read from Europe PMC abstracts (Masuki et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2019, 679 adults aged ~65; also PMC9024697, CC BY). Protocol: ≥5 sets of 3 min fast (≥70% peak VO2 for walking) and 3 min slow (~40%), ≥4 days/week. Credit the Shinshu group; the original trials used accelerometers to check intensity.
whoItsFor: Middle-aged and older adults who want more fitness than ordinary walking gives, without running. Studied in thousands of people aged ~60-75.
howToRun: Do at least 4 days a week; the studies aimed for about 60 minutes of fast walking per week.
Fast = as quick as you can walk until you're puffing and talking is hard (about 70% of your walking capacity).
Slow = a relaxed stroll to recover (about 40%).
You can split sets through the day; walking alone doesn't prevent falls, so add strength and balance work too.

name: 10-20-30 Running Intervals
description: Five-minute blocks of 30 s jog, 20 s steady, 10 s near-sprint, repeated 3-4 times with 2 minutes' rest.

exercises.name: Rest between blocks (each block = 5 x 30-20-10; 3-4 blocks)

credit: Gunnarsson TP & Bangsbo J, University of Copenhagen (J Appl Physiol 2012)
sourceNote: Read from the PubMed abstract via Europe PMC. Abstract: 3 or 4 x 5-min intervals of 30/20/10 s at <30/<60/>90% of max intensity, 2 min recovery between. 'sets' on the 30-20-10 rows = up to 4 blocks; each block repeats the 30-20-10 cycle 5 times. Warm-up not stated in the abstract.
whoItsFor: Moderately trained runners (the study group averaged VO2max 52) who want more speed on less weekly mileage.
howToRun: Warm up with easy jogging first (the abstract doesn't set a warm-up; ~10 min is typical).
Each block: 5 x [30 s easy, 20 s moderate, 10 s close to flat out], no break inside the block.
In the study this replaced all running for 7 weeks; most people do it 1-2 times a week with easy runs on other days.
Results reported: 5 km about 48 s faster, VO2max +4%, lower resting blood pressure.

name: NHS Physio Runner Strength & Flexibility
description: An NHS physiotherapy injury-prevention routine for runners: single-leg strength, core and calf work, plus three stretches.

exercises.name: Single-leg heel raise (straight knee, hold bench)

credit: Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (physiotherapy)
sourceNote: Free NHS trust page (© Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS FT). Page sets 3 sets of 3-10 reps, 2-3x/week unless stated; plank 15-60 s x2-3; stretches ~20 s x3. Exercise names and doses only; credit and link.
whoItsFor: Runners of any level who want a simple home routine to stay injury-free, especially beginners and returners.
howToRun: Do it 2-3 times a week on easy or non-running days.
3 sets of 3-10 reps unless stated; start at the low end and build.
Progress the bridge to single-leg when double-leg is easy.
Hold the kitchen bench for heel raises; stop anything that causes pain.

name: NHS Knee Exercises for Runners
description: Five quick NHS knee exercises to use as a running warm-up or cool-down: wall squats, thigh squeezes, hamstring stretch, squats and lunges.
credit: NHS
sourceNote: Free NHS guidance (© Crown copyright), reviewed 20 Sep 2024. Names and doses only; where the page gives no dose we say so. Credit and link to NHS.
whoItsFor: Runners without a current knee injury who want simple knee-strength work they can do anywhere.
howToRun: Use before a run as a warm-up or after as a cool-down.
Wall squats and squats have no set dose on the page - do slow, controlled reps you can manage pain-free.
Squat only to a right angle at the knee and keep your back straight.
You shouldn't feel pain; if you do, stop and get advice. Not for people with an existing knee injury.

name: Pat Carroll 15 x 30/30
description: Fifteen 30-second efforts at 80% with 30-second jog recoveries and an extra minute's jog after rep 10.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Newer half-marathon and 10K runners doing their first structured speed work; also the race-week sharpener in Pat's advanced plans.
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
Ideally the first and last fast 30 s cover the same ground.
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll 8 x 1 min / 30 s jog
description: Eight 1-minute efforts at 80% with only 30 seconds of jogging between, plus a minute's jog at halfway.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Half-marathon and marathon runners in the early weeks of a 12-week block.
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
Later in the block this becomes 10 x 1 min (extra jog after rep 5).
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll 6 x 2 min / 30 s jog
description: Six 2-minute efforts at 80% with short 30-second jog recoveries - a step up from the 1-minute session.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Intermediate half-marathoners mid-block.
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
Short recoveries are the point - don't stop and stand.
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll 15 Hill Reps
description: Fifteen ~30-second hill reps on a moderate slope, jogging back down, with a 1-minute standing rest after rep 10.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Road runners building strength and form for a half or full marathon (beginners in Pat's plans start with 10 reps).
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
Pick a hill you can run quickly all the way up - not so steep you labour. Drive off the balls of the feet, knees up, shoulders relaxed.
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll A-B-A 4 x 4 min
description: Out-and-back pacing reps: run 2 minutes out at 80%, turn, and try to arrive back at the start at exactly 4 minutes. 45 s standing rest.

exercises.name: A-B-A rep: 2 min out + 2 min back

credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Half and full marathoners learning even pacing without a GPS watch.
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
Back too early? You went out too slow. Not back in 4 min? Too fast. Aim for an even out-and-back.
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll A-B-A 5 + 5 + 10
description: Two 5-minute efforts out at 75% (30 s rest between), then a non-stop return at 80% - try to pass the start before 10 minutes.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery. Pat's notes say every speed session starts with a 10-15 min warm-up jog and ends with a cool-down jog and stretching. Credit Pat Carroll and link out.
whoItsFor: Experienced half-marathoners practising a negative-split, progressive effort.
howToRun: Run out of your comfort zone on the efforts; everything else stays relaxed and conversational.
Hold the same pace from the first rep to the last - if you slow badly, you started too fast.
The return leg has to be quicker than the outward 10 minutes - that's the test.
In Pat's plans this is one of two speed/hill sessions a week, with 1-3 rest or cross-training days.

name: Pat Carroll 6 x 500 m
description: Six 500 m efforts at 80% with 1-minute standing recoveries - the beginner half plan's measured session.
credit: Pat Carroll (Australian All-Comers half-marathon record holder, 61:11) for the Great Ocean Road Running Festival
sourceNote: Free 12-week plan PDF on the official Great Ocean Road Running Festival website (2017 edition); no copyright or reproduction notice. Effort percentages, reps and recoveries recorded as written; SR = standing recovery, JR = jog recovery.
